claims.text: High-temperature structural and chemical stability is governed by preservation of the nanoparticles' solid-solution structure.
High-temperature structural and chemical stability is governed by suppression of elemental segregation.
Optimization of synthesis conditions can preserve the solid solution and suppress elemental segregation.
Using in situ characterization can preserve the solid solution and suppress elemental segregation.
In situ transmission electron microscopy or X-ray absorption spectroscopy can monitor nanoparticle stability during thermal cycling.
Thermal cycling under vacuum or inert atmosphere can simulate catalytic and thermoelectric operating conditions.
Preservation of the solid-solution structure during thermal cycling maintains chemical and structural stability.
Suppression of elemental segregation during thermal cycling maintains chemical and structural stability.
Nanoparticles that preserve their solid-solution structure will exhibit improved high-temperature structural and chemical stability.
Nanoparticles that suppress elemental segregation will exhibit improved high-temperature structural and chemical stability.
Nanoparticles that undergo significant segregation or structural changes will degrade.
The proposed catalytic-operation boundary is 773–1173 K.
The proposed thermoelectric-use boundary is 473–1923 K.
The exact relationship among synthesis conditions, solid-solution structure, and high-temperature stability is unknown.
Degradation despite preservation of the solid-solution structure would falsify the proposed relationship between structure preservation and stability.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis presents in situ characterization as a means of achieving preservation and segregation suppression, whereas the intervention defines it only as a monitoring method; observation alone is not a controlled synthesis or stabilization intervention.
